block.heading: A maximum price on a diagram
block.text:
With bread at an equilibrium of N$14 and 500 loaves a day, a maximum price of N$12 cuts quantity supplied to 400 and raises quantity demanded to 600: a shortage of 200. Neither curve shifts.

![Maximum price on bread](diagrams/item-6145-6.3-017-proc-answer.png)

item.prompt: Bakeries in a town supply 300, 400, 500 and 600 loaves of bread a day at N$10, N$12, N$14 and N$16 a loaf, and consumers demand 700, 600, 500 and 400 loaves at those prices, as in the diagram. The government sets a maximum price of N$12 a loaf. Use the diagram to show the original equilibrium, the maximum price and its effect on the market (4).
item.canonical_answer: The original equilibrium E, where D meets S, is N$14 a loaf and 500 loaves a day. Draw the maximum price as a horizontal line at N$12, below the equilibrium price, so it is binding. Neither curve shifts: at N$12 quantity demanded, read off D, is 600 loaves and quantity supplied, read off S, is 400 loaves. Demand exceeds supply, so there is a shortage of 200 loaves a day. Only 400 loaves can be bought, fewer than the 500 before, so queues or an illegal market may develop.
